17.0.s.en: (1) The glory of the Father and the glory of the Son

17.0.0.en: After Christ finished His long previous talk with His disciples, He began a talk with the Father, and lifted up His eyes toward heaven to teach us, when we pray, to look to heaven, so that our thoughts may rise above earthly things. He declared the nearness of the hour of accomplishing redemption on the Cross, for He knows it beforehand, and became incarnate for it. "Glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee": the glory of the Son is the accomplishment of redemption on the Cross, and the glorifying of the Father is the accomplishment of His will, which is the salvation of mankind by redemption.

17.1.0.en: The glory of the Son in His incarnation was hidden, and so Christ begins here to declare some of the secrets of this glory: He is the only One who has authority over all creation, and He is the Giver of eternal life by redemption to everyone who believes in Him.

17.2.0.en: Eternal life is the knowledge of God and permanent existence with Him, and reaching it is through faith in Christ the Savior, who redeemed us on the Cross and taught us how to live with God on earth by His life.

17.3.0.en: Christ completed His mission and glorified the Father by fulfilling all the righteousness of the Law, and called people to the Kingdom of Heaven by continual talk about God the Father and how to live with Him. And finally by obeying the Father in offering Himself as a sacrifice on the wood of the Cross for the redemption of all mankind.

17.4.0.en: The glory of divinity belonged to the Son from eternity, was hidden by the Incarnation, and appeared in the Resurrection and Ascension.

17.4.1.en: May we fulfill the commandments of God, so that we taste the pledge of eternity on earth, and God may glorify us and make us rejoice in the Kingdom.

17.5.0.en: "I have manifested thy name": that is, by My speaking of You as Father. The Jews' knowledge of God was limited, and did not grasp the Trinity.

17.5.1.en: And through the incarnation of Christ they knew God more, and many of them followed Christ, holding fast to His commandments.

17.6.0.en: "All things whatsoever thou hast given me": that is, perfect wisdom, the teaching of the commandments, and all the miracles they saw, by which they became certain that Christ was sent from the Father and His word is the word of God, so their faith became firmer.

17.7.0.en: This does not mean that Christ does not pray for the world, for in (vv. 20, 21) He prays for the world that will believe in Him. Likewise on the wood of the Cross, He prays for those who crucified Him (see Lk 23:34). But He singled out His disciples here for prayer, because of the persecution and troubles to which they alone would be exposed as a result of the responsibility of preaching falling on them, and their need of a higher level of support.

17.8.0.en: He declares the equality of the Son with the Father in the ownership of all creation, that is, that Christ is God. Christ is glorified in His disciples by their keeping His commandments, then by their preaching in His name.

17.8.1.en: My beloved brother, the glorifying of the name of Christ and its proclamation did not become the responsibility of the disciples alone, but the responsibility of all the children of God. So a great task lies on us, which is to glorify the name of Christ before all those around us. And this will not come about except by our acting on His commandment, our constant repentance, and our striving against our lusts, so that our old man disappears (see Rom 6:6; Eph 4:22; Col 3:9), and in its place our Christ who dwells in us appears.

17.9.0.en: That is, the time and season of My mission and My work on earth has ended, but they are still remaining, and will meet much, and they also must show forth and glorify My name, and complete the preaching I began. Therefore I ask also for them that You keep them from evil, and from the world that they will face, and from all that awaits them. "Through thine own name": a metonym for the power and care of God, as the wise man says: "The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe" (Prov 18:10).

17.9.1.en: "That they may be one": that is, union at the level of heartfelt love, thought and purpose, without quarrel or division. How much the shepherds and servants need this petition now, for the peace of the Church and of those served is founded on the love of the servants and the unity of their thought. And how much the Church needs to pray for her shepherds, that God may keep them from the wars of division and partisanship.

17.9.2.en: "As we are": Christ's desire that the perfection of union among the disciples be as it is between the Father and the Son.

17.10.0.en: "While I was with them ... and now come I to thee": the two verses are connected and complete one meaning.

17.10.1.en: That is, during My presence, the disciples were in My keeping, and so My teaching, My guidance and My following up on them preserved them. But now that the time has come when I will leave the world, I return the responsibility of preserving them to Your name, O Father. And here I pray this before them, that they may have joy and confidence in the continuation of divine care for them, in the face of the distress and persecution that the world will bring upon them.

17.10.2.en: "The son of perdition": a clear reference to Judas. The Lord called him by this name to show Judas' evil will, that he is the one who deserved perdition, and did not benefit from the keeping care of Christ that kept the rest of the disciples.

17.10.3.en: "That the scripture might be fulfilled": as the prophecies in the Holy Bible (Ps 109:8; 41:9) mentioned about the betrayal of Judas and God's rejection of him.

17.11.0.en: Christ taught His disciples and His Church the word of God, which is exalted above the thoughts of the world and reveals its errors. Therefore the world hates all the children of God who hold fast to the pure and clean life, as it hated Christ also before them.

17.11.1.en: And what comforts us here is what St. Paul mentioned: "Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Tim 3:12).

17.12.0.en: Since the world hates the children of God, the solution is not that Christ lift them up with Him to heaven, but that He keep them and strengthen them in facing evil and the evil one. And Christ gives encouragement to the children of God, since He affirms their spiritual lineage to God, and not to the world.

17.13.0.en: Christ asks in His prayer that the disciples be established in all His words, the truth, which they heard from Him. And just as Christ set Himself apart, sanctified Himself, for teaching them and redeeming them, the turn comes to them also to be set apart, like their Lord, for being sent to the world and preaching redemption and the Kingdom of Heaven.

17.14.0.en: In His prayer here, the Lord Christ goes beyond the disciples to the whole Church in all her ages.

17.15.0.en: "That they all may be one": is the blood of redemption not one? Is the Teacher not one? Is the water of Baptism not one? So it is natural that we be one, not in form or outward appearance, but in thought and heartfelt love, on the pattern of the oneness between the Son and the Father, not in essence, but in love as far as we can according to our human nature.

17.16.0.en: "The glory which thou gavest me I have given them": the glory here is explained by St. John Chrysostom as authority and gifts, and sharing with Christ in the work of salvation by preaching. And the aim of giving this glory is also oneness. Just as the glory of the Father and the Son is one because they are one, Christ gave us this glory for the same purpose, that is, the oneness of the members and structure of the Church.

17.17.0.en: Christ rises to the highest levels of oneness, presenting a wonderful spiritual theological truth, explaining it thus: I am in them by My humanity, My incarnation and My sacrifice for them, and You are in Me with the fullness of Your divinity, and I am in You. For Christ joined and reconciled the Father with mankind in His blessed person; in Christ, humanity was united with God, and heaven with earth, and Christ became an intercessor and propitiatory mediator, which made the Father's love for mankind an extension of His love for His only Son.

17.17.1.en: By submitting to the commandments of God we become one in Him.

17.17.3.en: Verses 20-23 show God's concern for oneness in His Church. But the devil was able to divide the Church by means of pride. The solution is humility to reach oneness, while holding fast to the faith delivered by Christ and the Apostles.

17.18.0.en: The first petition was for their sanctification, and the second for their unity together and their union with Him. This third petition is for continual presence with Him, and it is the highest of the longings of Christ's love that He declares. Therefore the Lord used here the word "I will," and not "I ask"; for asking is a request, but "I will" adds the dimension of feelings, attachment and true care in having all His children with Him in His bosom. And as they shared in bearing the cross of persecution and the toil of preaching, they will also have fellowship in the glory of the Son (1 Cor 12:26).

17.18.1.en: "Before the foundation of the world": this shows the eternity of the Son (see ch. 1:1).

17.19.0.en: "The world hath not known thee": in the whole world, idolatry was dominant. And in Israel, the knowledge was theoretical and literal, without entering into the depth of the knowledge of God. But Christ's knowledge of the Father is eternal and of His very being. And the knowledge of the Father became available to all of us through His only Son. Christ pointed here to the faith of the disciples, by their receiving the Son, which is the first step in the knowledge of the Father that has begun, and which Christ will complete after the Resurrection, by explaining the things concerning the Kingdom. And the Holy Spirit completes our knowledge of the infinite Father, so our love for Him grows; and by this Christ abides in our hearts.

17.19.1.en: I thank You, my God, for Your great love, of which I have grasped only a little; grant me to respond to Your love, so that it is reflected as love for all those around me.

17.19.2.en: The arrest and trial of Jesus

18.0.0.en: The closing Passover discourse, which occupied chapters 14, 15 and 16, and likewise the prayer of the Lord Jesus to the Father in (ch. 17), ended, and the events of the last scene in the life of the Lord Jesus on earth began, with His going out to the garden of Gethsemane in the Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem toward the Mount of Olives, and He took His disciples with Him.

18.1.0.en: We note that St. John did not mention the details of Judas' agreement with the priests, or the price of the betrayal of the Lord, being content with what came in the other three Gospels, pointing to Judas' knowledge of the place where Christ gathered with the disciples in many retreats, and he also pictures the scene of the crowd coming out to arrest the Lord Jesus.

18.2.0.en: "Went forth ... knowing": ... that is, He went to death by Himself to meet it, and they did not enter to Him. St. John pointed to Christ's knowledge with a new sign to affirm His divinity, and He asked them what they wanted, which He knew well, and the answer of the Lord Christ, "I am he," shows us the reaction of the whole kingdom of darkness before God and His Word: they were soldiers and servants and crowds, and Christ was alone, and yet they drew back and fell to the ground, as though Christ were saying: You have no right to seize Me, unless I give Myself over to you to death.

18.3.0.en: Christ repeated the question, and they repeated the same answer, so this time He offered Himself for that for which He came, and did not fail to redeem His disciples, but asked that they be let go. St. John refers to what the Lord Christ had said before in (ch. 17:12) in His prayer to the Father, that none of them be lost.

18.4.0.en: See (Mt 26:51; Mk 14:47; Lk 22:50), but note that St. John mentioned the name of Peter and the name of the servant, which are not mentioned in the other three Gospels.

18.5.0.en: See (Mt 26:52, 54), and note that the Lord Christ rejected the human, emotional manner of what Peter did, making clear that there was a greater work that Christ had to accomplish, which was to accept the cup of suffering, that is, to accomplish redemption on the Cross.

18.6.0.en: "The band and the captain": that is, the Romans. Although they, with the servants of the Jews, formed a company, and Christ was alone, they bound Him, perhaps for fear of His escaping in the darkness, or in order to further put Him in the form of a guilty accused man, for malice had taken its share of them. And in the binding of Christ there is also a correspondence with the story of Isaac, whom Abraham bound to offer him as a sacrifice.

18.6.1.en: O Fashioner of all creation, its Redeemer and Liberator, they bound You willingly, though You are able to command legions of angels ... What love is this, that the guilty is set free and the innocent is taken bound ... Understand, O my soul, and if only you would understand.

18.7.s.en: (2) The meeting with Annas and Peter's denial

18.7.0.en: Caiaphas was the high priest, and his father-in-law Annas was also an earlier high priest, and every high priest keeps his title after the period of his high priesthood. The meeting with Annas was mentioned by John alone, while the other Gospels were content to mention the meeting with Caiaphas. Some hold that the meeting with Annas was a passing meeting on the way to Caiaphas, but the servants were careful for this quick meeting with Annas because of his old age, and his advanced honor as a former high priest. As for Caiaphas, his son-in-law, St. John wanted to remind us of him, for he was the one who gave the counsel that one man should die for the people (ch. 11:49, 50), and this reference has its importance in making clear that the Jewish trial was a sham, and that the decision for the death of the Lord Jesus had been premeditated.

18.8.0.en: John did not mention the flight of the disciples as Matthew did (Mt 26:56), but was content to mention that, with Peter, he followed Jesus. And because of John's connection with the priestly circle, he was able to enter inside the house. But Peter stood outside until he brought him in. However, before bringing him in, when Peter stood with the servants and guards warming themselves outside, St. John mentions the first incident of Peter's denial before the maid who questioned him, and he denied out of his fear before the crowd.

18.9.0.en: The questioner here is Annas, and the purpose of the question was that he might find a complaint against Christ to present to Caiaphas and the council after him. The subject of the question was Christ's teachings to the crowds, and His private teachings to His disciples. But the answer of Jesus came as a complete dispelling of Annas' hopes, for He had taught nothing in secret or in hiding, for all His teachings were heard by everyone, whether in the Temple, the synagogues or other places. Therefore also Christ answers with a question: "Why askest thou me?!" Ask rather all the crowds who heard Me!

18.10.0.en: One of the servants flared up, considering it an improper answer, and the hand of the wicked struck the face of the Righteous One, and this blow carried flattery to the high priest at the expense of truth and justice. Therefore the Lord Christ commented, rebuking the one who struck Him, for Christ had not sinned against the high priest according to the Law of Moses (Ex 22:28): "why smitest thou me?" That is, you, wicked servant, have become a breaker of the law, which I did not break...

18.10.1.en: In this text there are lessons to be learned:

18.10.2.en: The first: what did Christ endure for my salvation? Behold, God has become a spectacle to every gloater, struck by the hand of a servant. Shall I then endure people's insults to me?!

18.10.3.en: The second: there is no objection to the wronged person's making clear to the wrongdoer the wrong he has done him, so as to show him what he has fallen into, so long as that is with gentleness and love.

18.10.4.en: In this regard, St. Augustine wrote a wonderful reflection on this blow, saying: "Christ did not only turn His other cheek to be struck, but gave His whole body to be crucified, thereby fulfilling more than He taught in (Mt 5:39)."

18.11.0.en: The trial before Caiaphas was the official Jewish trial of Christ. Yet John did not focus on it, being content with what Matthew and Mark recorded of its details. But he mentioned what the two did not about the first meeting with Annas, then referred to Caiaphas and passed beyond him, taking Christ across to the official Roman trial before Pilate.

18.12.0.en: St. John mentions here the second and third denials of Peter, and the incident of the crowing of the cock, and his account was more detailed, for he brought out the first denial at Annas' house, and the second and third at Caiaphas' house. As for Matthew (26:69-73), Mark (14:66-71) and Luke (22:55-62), they summarized the three denials after the trial, so as not to interrupt the narrative, and so that the dialogue of the trial remained continuous.

18.12.1.en: It is also noted that St. John did not mention here Peter's oaths in denying, or Christ's looking at him, or his bitter weeping and repentance as came in the other three Gospels.

18.12.2.en: Many wonder how Peter denied You after these years, and what he saw and heard in them...?!

18.12.3.en: But perhaps Peter had an excuse in his fear, and in Your divinity's not yet being revealed by Your Resurrection, or the Holy Spirit's not yet having come upon him. What excuse have the many today, who declare with their tongues their faith and their following, but with their hearts and works deny You, and become a cause of others' blaspheming Your name?! Yes, my God ... forgive us and have mercy on us; how much we need the bitter tears of Peter.

18.13.s.en: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

18.13.0.en: As we said, St. John did not mention the details of Christ's trial before Caiaphas, in which He declared clearly that He is the Christ, the Son of God, which the Jews considered blasphemy (Mt 26:65; Mk 14:64; Lk 22:71). Nor did he mention the gathering of the rulers in the morning, the council of the Jews, and the taking of the decision, but moved us directly to the trial before Pilate.

18.13.1.en: "The judgment hall": a building built by Herod the Great, set aside for the lodging and residence of the Roman governor during his visits to Jerusalem. It was considered unclean by the Jews, because it belonged to the dwellings of the Gentiles, and therefore they did not enter it, but Pilate went out to them in the courtyard before the building, and asked them the reason for their gathering, and the reason for their complaint against the Lord Jesus. "That they might eat the passover": that is, the continuation of the Passover celebrations. But what truly amazes us is the leaders of the Jews' holding fast to formal bodily cleanness, while their hearts were plotting the betrayal of pure, innocent blood?!

18.14.0.en: The rulers of the Jews did not present an accusation against the Lord Jesus, but only wanted a decision for His death, and therefore they said to Pilate: "If he were not a malefactor."

18.14.1.en: That is, we have investigated and made sure that He must die, and all that remains for you is the decision, that is, the order for His crucifixion, over which we as Jews have no authority, but it is from your authority alone (crucifixion was under the authority of the Roman governor). But note Pilate's deliberateness, and his not rushing after their opinion.

18.15.0.en: "That ... might be fulfilled": that is, what Christ, to whom be glory, prophesied, that His death would be by the Cross, as came explicitly in (Mt 20:19), and implicitly in (Mk 10:21; Lk 9:23; 14:27), because if the Jews had judged Christ without Pilate, His death would have been by stoning. But everything that Christ prophesied had to be fulfilled to the letter. Therefore the Jews, in their malice, went to Pilate to have Him crucified, not knowing that by this they were fulfilling the highest divine will.

18.16.0.en: Pilate was alone with Christ, and asked Him about what had been raised by the priests and their servants, concerning Christ's claim about Himself that He is the king of the Jews, knowing that such an accusation alone is enough for the crucifixion of Christ, for kingship belongs to Caesar alone, and any attempt to attribute kingship to another is considered rebellion and a coup. But Christ did not answer, but replied with a new question, which is considered a warning and an awakening of Pilate's conscience. The meaning of Christ's question: Is this your own opinion, or are you repeating the accusations these men have reported to you about Me, so that you may find a reason to try Me?

18.17.0.en: "Am I a Jew?": a question of protest, in which Pilate makes clear his position, that he does not consider Christ a king, for he is not a Jew; as though he were saying: I have nothing to do with all this, for these are the words of the Jews. Some see that the saying "Am I a Jew?" means a protest and a stirring up of Roman pride against the nation of the Jews, over their having a king other than Caesar, king of the whole ancient world. Pilate continues his inquiry of Christ with his experience as an investigator: "What hast thou done?", especially since the whole Jewish nation, that is, the great crowds outside the judgment hall, had delivered You up, complaining against You?!

18.18.0.en: Christ defends Himself against the accusation the chief priests attached to Him.

18.18.1.en: But this defense is not intended to avert the Cross for which He came and became incarnate, but to teach us all a spiritual rule and constitution. If Christ our King declares to us that He does not belong to this world, but has another, heavenly, eternal kingdom, then what should the state of His subjects be but that they too rise above this world with all its lusts, and say, as Christ said before: "We are from above; we are not of this world" (see ch. 8:23), and that the world not rule over us in anything, but that we seek the heavenly Kingdom of our God.

18.18.2.en: And Christ adds a proof to His words, that if He were an earthly king, He would have cared to have servants and guards to defend Him, so that the Jews would not seize Him, but on the contrary, He asked to give Himself over gently in exchange for the release of the disciples.

18.19.0.en: "Art thou a king then?": a question that expresses bewilderment and wonder. For Christ declares that He is a king, and denies the earthly kingdom that Pilate understands. His answer came affirming the spiritual meaning of His kingdom, for He did not deny being a king, but adds that He became incarnate to redeem mankind and to reign over its heart.

18.19.1.en: "Every one that is of the truth": that is, everyone who received My word and the work of the Holy Spirit within him, or everyone who is subject to God, who is the Truth, and knew Christ as the sheep know the voice of the shepherd and follow him (ch. 10:4).

18.20.0.en: "What is truth?": Pilate did not understand the words that Christ spoke. Therefore he asked a question and did not wait to hear its answer, as though he were in truth not concerned to understand ... but it was merely a question. Without doubt, Pilate found no cause in Christ that deserved death. Therefore he went out again to the Jews who were waiting outside, declaring the first verdict of innocence, that he found in Him no fault at all. Perhaps God made Pilate utter this very sentence to show one thing: Christ is the true Passover, who is without a single blemish, and He is the sacrifice for sin, which also required that it be without blemish ... So what Pilate uttered is nothing but a confirmation of the perfection of the sacrifice of Christ that was offered.

18.21.0.en: Pilate erred when he abandoned the duties of his office, as a judge of truth, in releasing the one he saw to be innocent, but gave up his authority in judgment, and gave the right of choice to the people, which was unheard of, and thought that his declaring Christ's innocence relieved him of the responsibility that he left to the people. Perhaps he thought that by opening the door of choice, they would ask for the release of the one in whom there was no fault, but the surprise was in their asking for the release of one known to be a robber and an insurrectionist.

18.21.1.en: How strange a people that released a robber and crucified a righteous man!!

18.21.2.en: Pilate's gross error gives all of us a lesson in witnessing to the truth. Politicians may bargain or strike deals, and the limits of truth become very wide. But the children of God are not so; rather, truth is truth, for "he that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD" (Prov 17:15).

18.21.3.en: The crucifixion, death and burial of Christ
